He stressed on open architecture, secure data, adaptable systems, cost-effective counter-drone measures and an AI industrial base. Bhattacharya, President, Centre for Digital Economy Policy Research (C-DEP), said India's growing reliance on networked systems, data and artificial intelligence makes open architecture and interoperability increasingly important for the armed forces. items.article: M att Parker and Trey Stone t ake aim at the obscenely wealthy in the latest episode – but it feels harder now to forget how wealthy they are A little over a year ago, South Park creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone renewed their deal with Paramount after a contentious negotiation that held up production of the 2025 season. That $1.5bn agreement raised questions about whether Paramount, newly owned by David Ellison, would really offer the creators creative freedom – or was the billionaire class solidifying its hold over a comedy series as cover to meddle in other divisions, like CBS News? The deal also made Parker and Stone likely billionaires themselves. Between this renewal and their co-ownership of the South Park intellectual property, they each have an estimated net worth of over $1bn. The second episode of the show’s 29th season examines life from either side of the billionaire/regular people divide. On one hand, Parker and Stone are unsparing of their corporate benefactors, depicting billionaires as tiny, sentient penises with high-pitched voices who are addicted to sharing their stupid opinions on podcasts and social media in their miniature city called Billionaire Weenietown. On the other hand, Parker and Stone aren’t exactly taking shots from outside Weenietown. Though they were certainly famous before becoming billionaires, they were still outside that world. But one of its lesser-known treasures is Badam ki Jali,” he wrote. “A 200-year-old Nizami-era sweet, it’s made with almonds, sugar and cardamom, delicately patterned and baked. items.text: New driving licence changes start today. Here's what they could mean for you
items.article: Learners must now spend at least six months getting driving experience before they can take a practical test Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. New driving licence restrictions have come into effect banning young people from carrying certain passengers at night and restricting when learner drivers can take a test. The changes, which have been launched in Northern Ireland, are aimed at reducing fatal road crashes involving young people. According to official figures, 17- to 23-year-old drivers were responsible for almost a quarter of all collisions in Northern Ireland in 2024. That is despite them only accounting for 8 per cent of licence holders. Data also shows that 251 people were killed or seriously injured in collisions involving a young driver in 2024. In 65 per cent of cases, the young driver was at fault. The changes come after the government announced in January that learner drivers in England and Wales could face a wait of six months between sitting their theory and practical tests.
